Alhazen / Ibn al-Haytham

No medieval thinker is more important to the computational neuroscience of perception than Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen, c. 965–1040). In his monumental Kitāb al-Manāẓir 1, he established that vision works by light entering the eye (refuting the extramission theory) and, crucially, that perception involves unconscious judgment and inference. The optical image on the crystalline humor is insufficient to determine the scene: the mind must draw on prior experience, comparison, and recognition to construct a percept. This is, in all but mathematical formalism, the hypothesis that perception is inference—the core of the Helmholtzian and Bayesian traditions—articulated seven centuries before Helmholtz.

Avicenna / Ibn Sina

Avicenna (Ibn Sina, c. 980–1037) elaborated Aristotle’s brief remarks on inner sense into a detailed faculty psychology 2, 3. Between raw sensation and abstract intellection, he posited a cascade of internal senses: the common sense (integrating modalities), retentive and compositive imagination (storing and recombining images), wahm (estimation—the immediate, pre-rational detection of significance, as when a sheep perceives danger in a wolf’s form), and memory. His celebrated floating man thought experiment—a person created in midair, deprived of all sensation, who would nonetheless know that he exists—argues that self-awareness is prior to and independent of any world model.

Averroes / Ibn Rushd

Averroes (Ibn Rushd, c. 1126–1198) produced the most influential medieval commentaries on Aristotle’s De Anima 4, which shaped European scholastic psychology for centuries. His most provocative thesis was that the agent intellect—the faculty that renders sensory particulars into universal concepts—is a single, supra-individual entity shared by all humans. Whatever its metaphysical plausibility, this raises a question that computational neuroscience still grapples with: to what extent are the abstract representational structures of cognition universal across brains?

Thomas Aquinas

Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274) synthesized Aristotelian psychology with Christian theology to produce a theory of cognition as abstraction 5, 6. The intellect does not know material objects directly; it abstracts intelligible species (structural forms) from phantasms (sensory images) produced by the internal senses. This process—from high-dimensional sensory data to compressed, abstract, category-level representations—is a medieval description of what we would now call hierarchical feature extraction.

William of Ockham

William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347) contributed two ideas of lasting relevance. First, his famous razor—entia non sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitatem—is a parsimony principle that, reformulated in information-theoretic terms, is central to Bayesian model selection and the free energy principle: the best model is one that explains the data with minimal complexity. Second, his theory of mental language (oratio mentalis) 7 proposed that thought occurs in an internal combinatorial language with its own syntax—anticipating Fodor’s language of thought hypothesis by six centuries.

Al-Farabi (c. 872–950), known in the Latin West as Alpharabius, developed an emanationist theory of intellect that doubles as a hierarchical model of cognitive processing 8, 9. Cognition proceeds through successive stages: from sensation, through imagination, to the various levels of intellect (potential, actual, acquired, and agent). Each stage abstracts further from the material particulars of sensation, progressively approaching purely intelligible form. This ascending hierarchy of abstraction—from low-level sensory features to increasingly general, amodal representations—maps with surprising precision onto the deep hierarchical architecture of modern generative models, where each layer learns progressively more abstract representations of its inputs. Roger Bacon

Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1294) synthesized Alhazen’s optics with Aristotelian natural philosophy in his Opus Majus 10, insisting that scientia experimentalis—knowledge grounded in systematic observation and experiment—must take priority over purely deductive reasoning. His theory of the multiplication of species described how causal influence propagates from objects through intervening media to the sense organs: every natural agent emits species (likenesses of itself) that are transmitted through the medium in straight lines, weakening with distance and undergoing refraction at boundaries. This is, in effect, a medieval theory of information propagation—an account of how structured signals from the distal environment are transmitted, transformed, and finally received by the brain’s sensory interfaces.
